title: Denoising Single-Atom Potentials
text: Bayesian, Gaussian-process, and multiscale methods for extracting physics from noisy molecular-dynamics signals.

title: Denoising Single-Atom Potentials
text:
The challenge
Single-atom electrostatic potentials fluctuate strongly in molecular simulations. The signal of interest can be smaller than the instantaneous thermal noise, and straightforward averaging can erase the local structure that gives the signal physical meaning.

title: Denoising Single-Atom Potentials
text:
The approach
This project combines structured probabilistic models with multiscale signal processing. The goal is not only to smooth a trajectory, but to quantify uncertainty and preserve the time and length scales that connect molecular fluctuations to interfacial response.

title: Denoising Single-Atom Potentials
text:
Current status
Model comparison and physical validation are ongoing. Notes and code from this work appear on GitHub as individual pieces become usable on their own.

title: About
text:
What I do
My research combines statistical physics, high-performance molecular simulation, and modern machine learning. I build models that connect microscopic motion to experimentally meaningful observables—especially electric fields, solvent organization, and electrochemical response at solid–liquid interfaces.
I’m most at home when a problem demands several kinds of thinking at once: physical theory to frame the question, computation to test it, and careful inference to separate signal from noise.

title: The 404 page is doing Bayesian inference
text: The spins on this site’s 404 page and home page are a biased Ising model. An external field shaped like the text pushes spins up inside the glyphs and down outside them, and the lattice is cooled until the pattern condenses out of thermal noise. The same equations, read differently, are one of the classic methods for restoring noisy images.

title: The 404 page is doing Bayesian inference
text:
Prior, likelihood, posterior
Take a binary picture \(x\), one value \(x_i = \pm 1\) per pixel. A reasonable prior belief about pictures is that neighboring pixels tend to agree, which is exactly what an Ising model says:
\[
p(x) \propto \exp\Big( J \sum_{\langle ij \rangle} x_i x_j \Big).
\]
Now observe the picture through a noisy channel that flips each pixel independently with probability \(p\). For one pixel, \(p(y_i \mid x_i)\) is \(1-p\) if \(y_i = x_i\) and \(p\) otherwise, which can be written as
\[
p(y_i \mid x_i) \propto \exp\big( h \, x_i y_i \big), \qquad h = \tfrac{1}{2} \ln \frac{1-p}{p}.
\]
Bayes’ rule multiplies the two:
\[
p(x \mid y) \propto \exp\Big( J \sum_{\langle ij \rangle} x_i x_j + \sum_i h_i x_i \Big), \qquad h_i = h \, y_i.
\]
That is a biased Ising model at \(k_B T = 1\). The coupling is the prior, and the external field is the data: each observed pixel pulls its spin toward what was seen, with a strength set by how much the channel can be trusted.

title: The 404 page is doing Bayesian inference
section: Gibbs sampling a picture of Gibbs
text:
Gibbs sampling a picture of Gibbs
To draw samples from this posterior, visit each pixel in turn and set it from its conditional distribution given its neighbors,
\[
P(x_i = +1 \mid \text{rest}) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\big[-2\big(J \sum_{j \in \partial i} x_j + h_i\big)\big]}.
\]
Physicists call this heat-bath dynamics. Geman and Geman, who introduced this approach to image restoration in 1984, called it the Gibbs sampler, after the Gibbs distribution it samples. So the default picture below is Gibbs himself.
The hidden picture is binarized (for the portraits, with a little edge enhancement so they read as pen sketches rather than silhouettes), flipped at random to make the observation, and then sampled from the posterior. The last panel averages the samples; its sign at each pixel is the estimate that minimizes the expected number of wrong pixels.

title: The 404 page is doing Bayesian inference
text:
Things to try

Set \(J = 0\). The prior disappears and every pixel is on its own. The posterior mean just agrees with the observation, so the error equals the flip probability.
Raise \(J\) slowly. Neighbors start voting, isolated flips get outvoted, and the error drops well below \(p\).
Keep going past \(J \approx 0.44\). That is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(1+\sqrt{2})\), the critical coupling of the two-dimensional Ising model, beyond which the prior on its own would order the whole lattice. The best reconstructions sit just above it, around \(J \approx 0.5\). Push further and the prior starts erasing real detail (eyes, glasses, beard texture, the water around the helix) and the error climbs again.
Push \(p\) toward 0.5. The field \(h\) goes to zero, the data stop carrying information, and the posterior relaxes back to the prior.

The trade-off in the third item has a physical reading I ran into while tuning the lattice on the 404 page. A feature survives only if the field energy it gains outweighs the domain-wall energy it costs: a stroke has to be wider than about \(2J/h\) pixels, and a hole enclosed by a stroke needs an area-to-perimeter ratio above about \(J/h\). In the statistical reading, the same inequality says how much evidence a small feature needs before the prior stops smoothing it away. That is a bias–variance trade-off in a physicist’s vocabulary.
The same question, of how much structure to assume and what it costs you, comes up whenever physics is recovered from noisy data, as in denoising single-atom potentials.

title: The 404 page is doing Bayesian inference
text:
Further reading

S. Geman and D. Geman, Stochastic relaxation, Gibbs distributions, and the Bayesian restoration of images, IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 6, 721–741 (1984).
J. Besag, On the statistical analysis of dirty pictures, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 48, 259–279 (1986). Introduces iterated conditional modes, a fast deterministic alternative to sampling.
D. M. Greig, B. T. Porteous, and A. H. Seheult, Exact maximum a posteriori estimation for binary images, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 51, 271–279 (1989). Shows the most probable image can be found exactly with a minimum cut.

Portraits of J. Willard Gibbs (before 1903) and Ludwig Boltzmann (1902) are in the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. The helix frame is from the replica-exchange simulations described on the helix–coil project page.

title: Nucleation you can poke
text: On this site’s home page, the lattice spells one word after another, and every change of word briefly heats the lattice. Without that pulse the old word does not go away. The field under it has reversed, so it is no longer the equilibrium state, but at low temperature it is metastable: nothing local can undo it, because every small change costs more than it gains. Getting out of a metastable state takes a rare, collective event, which is nucleation.

title: Nucleation you can poke
text:
The critical droplet
Start with every spin pointing down in a field \(h > 0\) that favors up. Flipping a roughly circular droplet of radius \(R\) gains \(2h\) per spin in the bulk but pays a surface tension \(\sigma\) along its edge. In the continuum approximation of classical nucleation theory,
\[
\Delta F(R) = 2\pi R\,\sigma - 2\pi h R^2 .
\]
The surface term wins for small droplets and the bulk term for large ones, so \(\Delta F\) has a maximum at the critical radius
\[
R^* = \frac{\sigma}{2h}, \qquad \Delta F^* = \frac{\pi \sigma^2}{2h}.
\]
Droplets smaller than \(R^*\) tend to shrink and larger ones tend to grow. For the square-lattice Ising model the surface tension along a lattice axis is known exactly from Onsager’s solution: \(\sigma(T) = 2J + k_BT \ln\tanh(J/k_BT)\), which falls to zero at \(T_c\). The widget below uses that value to estimate \(R^*\). It is only a guide: real droplets on a lattice are not circles, and the surface tension depends on the direction of the interface.

title: Nucleation you can poke
text:
Things to try

Plant droplets on either side of \(R^*\). At the default \(T = 1\) and \(h = 0.2\) the estimate is 4.3 cells, and the lattice agrees surprisingly well: in my runs, droplets of radius 4 or less melted back and droplets of radius 5 or more grew. Watch a growing droplet and it turns into a rounded square, the lattice anisotropy that the circular estimate ignores.
Just wait. At \(T = 1\), \(h = 0.2\) the barrier is about \(23\,J\), so spontaneous nucleation essentially never happens on this lattice. Raise \(h\) or \(T\) and the barrier drops quickly; at \(T = 1\), somewhere between \(h = 0.5\) and \(0.6\), droplets start appearing on their own within seconds.
Sweep the field. The magnetization lags behind the field and traces a hysteresis loop, switching only once the field is strong enough for nucleation to happen on the timescale of the sweep. The loop is not a property of the material alone: it depends on how fast the field moves compared to how long nucleation takes.
Heat toward \(T_c\). The surface tension vanishes, \(R^*\) collapses, and the loop closes.

Classical nucleation theory, with a critical nucleus set by the competition between surface and bulk free energy, is also the usual starting point for real clusters. That includes the ligand-mediated nanocluster growth in two of my papers (2019, 2020). This lattice is about the simplest system where you can watch the same idea play out spin by spin.

title: Reaction-Field Toolkit
text: A working collection of derivations and numerical experiments that connect continuum reaction-field theory with atomistic models.

title: Reaction-Field Toolkit
text:
The question
Continuum electrostatics offers elegant descriptions of polarization and screening, while molecular simulation resolves the discrete structure those descriptions average over. The useful physics often lives in the connection between the two.

title: Reaction-Field Toolkit
text:
The approach
This project develops spectral Green-function representations, identifies limits in which familiar reaction-field expressions emerge, and tests the resulting predictions against molecular simulation. The emphasis is on derivations that remain numerically tractable and easy to validate.

title: Reaction-Field Toolkit
text:
Current status
The derivations and validation suite are in active development. Working code appears on GitHub as the numerical experiments settle.

title: Helices in Nanotubes
text: Replica-exchange simulations of peptides inside carbon nanotubes open to a water reservoir: when does confinement fold a chain into a helix, and what role does the water play?

title: Helices in Nanotubes
text:
The question
Nascent proteins leave the ribosome through a narrow tunnel, and chaperonins fold proteins inside enclosed cavities. Confinement on this scale changes the balance of forces that decides secondary structure, but it also changes the water around the chain. Separating the two effects requires a system where both the pore and the solvent can be controlled.

title: Helices in Nanotubes
text:
The approach
Replica-exchange molecular dynamics (GROMACS) of capped polyalanine, polyserine, and polyglutamine in carbon nanotubes open to a water reservoir, mapping helix formation as a function of tube diameter and hydrophobicity. Comparing each system in the gas phase and in water isolates the solvation free-energy difference between the helix and coil states.

title: Helices in Nanotubes
text:
What we found

A helix forms only within a narrow window of tube diameters, one that is comparable to the width of the ribosome tunnel.
Inside the tube, helix formation in polyalanine is driven by a small negative enthalpy and a positive entropy change near 300 K, the opposite of bulk water, where a large entropy loss favors the coil.
Water density inside the tube is anticorrelated with structure formation, and more hydrophobic tubes enhance helicity.
Confinement stabilizes helices of chains with hydrophobic side chains, consistent with an entropic mechanism from polymer physics. Hydrophilic chains can also form helices, but whether they do depends on the tube through water-mediated interactions.
